newsitem.title: GERMANY: German health minister wants 50,000 cows killed.
newsitem.headline: German health minister wants 50,000 cows killed.

text.p: Bonn's Health Minister called on Wednesday for every German cow descended from British stock -- a total of up to 50,000 cattle -- to be slaughtered to prevent the spread of mad cow disease.

German fears of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) have surged in recent weeks with the first discovery of the illness in a calf believed to have been born in Germany, and the death of a woman aged 41, apparently from BSE-related brain disease.

The Agriculture Ministry has already ordered the slaughter of over 5,000 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland, where BSE is also widespread, and says 14,000 direct offspring must be killed if the calf is found to have inherited BSE.

But Health Minister Horst Seehofer told journalists on Wednesday, after reporting to the parliamentary health and agriculture committees, that "all the descendants of the imported animals must be slaughtered".
He said this should happen regardless of genetic tests to show whether the dead calf was infected by its mother -- something scientists have not yet proved to be possible.
Pressed to say whether he meant subsequent generations, he said "Yes". His ministry estimated this could mean 40,000 to 50,000 cattle, including those already earmarked for slaughter.

The Agriculture Ministry, however, wants to slaughter only 14,000 first-generation offspring of British and Swiss imports, and only if "maternal transmission" is shown to be likely. The genetic test could take up to 10 days.

There have already been calls for tighter bookkeeping after official records showed the calf's mother to have died healthy -- suggesting either that the records had been manipulated or the calf had eaten contaminated fodder made of animal protein.
Infected fodder is blamed for most if not all of Britain's 165,000 BSE cases, but Germany says such fodder is barely used here and is very unlikely to have been given to the calf.

Beef consumption in Germany has never recovered a slump prompted by Britain's announcement last year that it believed the deaths of several unusually young people from Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) were probably caused by contact with BSE-infected beef.
